summary: Describes ways RA-Guard implementations can be evaded using IPv6 extension headers and updates RFC 6105 so those evasion vectors are eliminated. The original RA-Guard mechanism is the one from RFC 6105.

plainLanguage.summary: Some RA-Guard devices can miss forged IPv6 Router Advertisements when they do not inspect the full packet header chain. RFC 7113 gives filtering rules to address those evasion methods.

questions: what are ipv6 rogue router advertisements
subtitle: Implementation rules to prevent IPv6 extension-header evasion of RA-Guard

tldr.problem: Some RA-Guard devices inspect only part of an IPv6 packet and can miss forged Router Advertisements hidden behind extension headers or fragmentation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires parsing the full IPv6 header chain, specifies how to handle incomplete first fragments and unknown Next Header values, and lists conditions under which packets must pass.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7113 updates RFC 6105 with implementation advice intended to eliminate the described evasion methods.

today: RFC 7113 updates RFC 6105, as recorded in the batch metadata. It is an Informational document that provides implementation advice for RA-Guard.

sections.title: Why Some RA-Guard Devices Can Be Evaded
sections.content:
IPv6 Router Advertisement Guard (RA-Guard) filters Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6 (ICMPv6) Router Advertisements at a Layer 2 device. The device must identify these messages reliably to block those arriving on ports that are not allowed to send them.

Some implementations inspect only the fixed IPv6 header's Next Header field. An attacker can place extension headers before the Router Advertisement, so a device that does not follow the full header chain may fail to recognize it. Fragmentation can also split the relevant headers across packets.
sections.plainLanguage: RA-Guard works only if the device can recognize a Router Advertisement. Extension headers and fragments can hide that message from devices that inspect only part of a packet.

sections.title: The Filtering Rules
sections.content:
On ports that are not allowed to send Router Advertisements, RA-Guard must pass packets whose source address is not link-local or whose Hop Limit is not 255. For other packets, it must parse the entire IPv6 header chain to identify the upper-layer message; an implementation with a byte-inspection limit must pass the packet when it reaches that limit and cannot claim compliance.

RA-Guard must drop a first fragment with Fragment Offset zero if it does not contain the entire IPv6 header chain. It must also drop identified Router Advertisements and packets with an unrecognized Next Header value. A configuration setting for unknown values must default to drop. Other packets pass as usual, and drops should be logged with a dedicated counter.
sections.plainLanguage: The device must inspect the full header chain before deciding whether a packet contains a Router Advertisement. It must drop an incomplete first fragment and an identified Router Advertisement on a blocked port.

sections.title: Fragment Handling and Remaining Risks
sections.content:
The incomplete-header rule applies to first fragments only. Later fragments may pass, because they cannot reassemble into a complete Router Advertisement when the required first fragment has been dropped. The RFC warns that a receiving host could retain buffers for fragments that never form a complete datagram if it does not manage reassembly resources properly.

Hosts that accept overlapping fragments may remain vulnerable to Router Advertisement attacks. The RFC identifies prohibiting fragmentation of Router Advertisements, as specified by RFC 6980, as the most effective mitigation, while noting that this requires implementation updates. Similar evasion techniques can affect protections against rogue DHCPv6 messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Dropping the incomplete first fragment stops the Router Advertisement from being reassembled. A receiver still needs to manage memory used for fragments that never complete.

sections.title: Scope of the Protection
sections.content:
RFC 7113 describes evasion techniques and filtering advice for RA-Guard. Its rules assume that hosts reject Router Advertisements with a non-link-local source address or a Hop Limit other than 255, as required by Neighbor Discovery.

RA-Guard addresses attacks based on Router Advertisement messages. Protection against similar attacks using other message types, including DHCPv6, is outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: These rules protect against Router Advertisement evasion. They do not define protection for other IPv6 messages, such as DHCPv6.
